messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ramesh sat across from me with the stillness of a man who had learned to be invisible. At seventy-five, his hands bore the permanent grey of clay worked into the creases, but they rested motionless on his knees, palms up, as though waiting for something to be placed into them. He had come to the clinic at his wife’s insistence, though he could not say what he hoped for. What he could say, haltingly, was that for the past several months he had felt as though he no longer existed as the person he had been. He was a potter—had been a potter since he was twelve years old in Sri Lanka, apprenticed to his uncle in a village north of Jaffna. He had built a life in the United States over thirty years, had raised children here, had taught ceramics at a community center. But now, he said, he could not bring himself to touch the wheel. The clay sat in bags in his garage, hardening. When his wife asked why he no longer worked, he told her he did not have the strength. What he meant was that he no longer knew who would sit down at that wheel.

The event that had undone him happened in 1983, during the Black July pogroms. Ramesh had been a young man then, living with his parents and younger sister in a mixed neighborhood. He remembered the sound first—the crackle of burning shops, the shouting that moved like a wave through the streets. He remembered the police truck that pulled up, and the officer who got out and looked at them not with anger but with something worse, a kind of recognition. Ramesh had been told to lie face down on the ground, and he had done so, and he had listened to his sister being pulled from the house. He had not moved. He had not moved because he believed that if he stayed still, if he made himself small and obedient, they would leave and everything would be fine. His sister had been seventeen. He never saw her again. For forty years he had told himself this story in a way that made it bearable: he had survived, he had built a new life, the past was the past. But in the last year, something had broken. He had attended a funeral for an old friend, and standing at the graveside, the smell of wet earth had hit him with a force that buckled his knees. The memory came not as a story but as a physical assault—the grit of dirt against his cheek, the weight of a boot on his spine, the sound of his sister’s voice calling his name. He could not speak of it afterward. When his wife asked what was wrong, he could only shake his head. The words would not come. The memory existed in his body, in his senses, but it had no language.

Since that funeral, Ramesh had become a man who watched. He scanned every room he entered, every street he walked, every parking lot. He checked the faces of passing drivers, the posture of strangers, the direction of their hands. He was certain that danger could arrive without warning, and that only constant vigilance would keep it at bay. He had stopped driving altogether because the sound of a car backfiring, or even a loud engine, sent his heart into his throat and left him shaking in his seat. He avoided the neighborhood where the Sri Lankan temple was located because he had seen a police car there one afternoon and had turned around and walked home without knowing why, only knowing that he could not go closer. He had also begun to avoid anything that might make him feel hope. When his grandson invited him to a school art show, Ramesh declined. When his wife suggested they take a weekend trip to the mountains, he said he was too tired. He had come to believe that any moment of happiness was a trap, a vulnerability that would be punished. Better to stay flat, to feel nothing, to keep the world at arm’s length. The only thing he allowed himself was the scanning—the endless, exhausting search for the threat that was surely coming.

His wife had noticed the changes. He no longer laughed at her jokes. He flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind. He had started sleeping in the guest room because he could not bear the vulnerability of lying still beside her in the dark. She had found him one night standing at the window, staring at the street, and when she asked what he was watching for, he had said, “I don’t know. But I have to watch.” It was this that finally brought them here. Ramesh did not believe that talking would help. He was certain that he had already failed the only test that had ever mattered, and that nothing could undo that. But he had come because his wife had cried, and he could not bear to see her cry. What he wanted, he said quietly, was to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life. He wanted to sit at his wheel again. He wanted to be able to close his eyes without seeing the earth. He did not know if such a thing was possible, but he had come anyway, and that, for a man who had spent forty years learning not to hope, was perhaps the bravest thing he had done in decades.
